title: PRD: Status page transparency upgrades (components + comms templates + post-incident summaries)
creator: Paula Mendes
description:
## Summary
Customers (and Support) repeatedly report that the public status page is too coarse to be useful during partial degradations (e.g., streaming-only issues, embeddings failures, region-limited impact). This PRD defines a cross-functional initiative to upgrade status page transparency across:
1) **Component granularity** (product surface x region x capability where appropriate)
2) **Standard incident communication templates** (clear, consistent, non-sensitive)
3) **Publishable post-incident summaries** that can be shipped quickly and linked from Console

The goal is to make availability reporting more precise, consistent, and actionable without increasing on-call burden or disclosing sensitive customer/capacity details.

---

## Problem statement
### What customers experience today
- Status page shows “API Degraded” even when only **Streaming** is impacted, or marks “Operational” while **Embeddings** requests fail.
- Regional issues (e.g., us-east only) get reported globally, causing unnecessary alarm and support load.
- Incident updates are inconsistent in tone/content; initial updates are sometimes delayed because teams debate what can be said and which components to mark.
- Post-incident writeups vary widely; customers ask for consistent summaries with impact and mitigations but without proprietary details.

### Evidence / inputs
- Support tickets highlighting mismatches:
  - SUP-28411 “status page missing embeddings component”
  - SUP-28436 “disputed status accuracy during us-east degradation”
  - SUP-28549 “streaming disconnects not reflected on status”
- Incident comms gaps called out in postmortems:
  - 2025-11-07 us-east streaming degradation (component too coarse; delayed/uncertain first update)
- Prospect feedback (enterprise procurement/security reviews):
  - Requests for per-region component status + predictable comms cadence and publishable post-incident summaries

---

## Goals (what success looks like)
1) **Accuracy:** Public status reflects the impacted product surface and region with minimal over-broad flagging.
2) **Speed:** Faster time-to-first-update (TTFU) with consistent initial messaging even when root cause is unknown.
3) **Consistency:** Standard wording across incident phases; less time spent debating what to say.
4) **Actionability:** Customers can tell whether the issue affects them (region + capability), and Support can point to a credible, consistent source.
5) **Low on-call overhead:** Templates + automation reduce manual work; avoid flapping statuses.

---

## Non-goals
- Committing to new SLAs or contractual availability changes (this is transparency/reporting, not an SLA expansion).
- Publishing customer-specific impact details (no tenant names, no customer-specific capacity constraints).
- Building a fully automated “no-human-in-the-loop” incident publisher for Sev0/Sev1 (we will add guardrails/approval where needed).
- Replatforming the status page vendor.

---

## Target users
- **Customers** (engineers + incident managers) who use status.redwoodinference.com to assess impact.
- **Support/CS** who need a clear authoritative source and reusable language for escalations.
- **On-call engineers / Incident Commanders / Comms Leads** who must update the status page quickly and safely.

---

## Scope
### 1) Public component taxonomy (status page)
We will introduce a canonical component model that supports:
- Product surfaces: Hosted API, Streaming, Embeddings, Reranking, Console
- Region splits (initial): us-east, us-west, eu-west (exact list finalized in taxonomy doc)
- Capability splits where necessary (e.g., Streaming as distinct from Chat completions)
- Dedicated and Private: follow policy defined in PM-612 (generally conservative public messaging; avoid tenant-specific statuses)

Acceptance criteria:
- Component list is understandable to customers (names aligned with docs/SDKs).
- Each component has an owner (SRE/Infra/Product area) and a mapping rule from internal signals.
- Changes to taxonomy are governed (review + safe rollout), with a single source of truth.

### 2) Incident communication templates
Standard templates for:
- Investigating
- Identified
- Mitigating
- Monitoring
- Resolved (+ link to post-incident summary when available)

Templates must include:
- Impacted components/regions
- Customer-visible symptoms (errors, elevated latency, streaming disconnects)
- What we’re doing (without sensitive details)
- Next update expectation (when appropriate)
- Clear “what we can/can’t say” guidance

### 3) Publishable post-incident summaries
A lightweight format that can be published quickly after resolution:
- Impact (what, who/where at a component/region level)
- Timeline (high-level)
- Root cause class (non-sensitive)
- Mitigation and prevention actions
- Links (status incident, optional RCA details if/when available)

### 4) Console integration (visibility + linking)
From Redwood Console:
- Link to relevant status incidents and post-incident summaries
- Ensure Dedicated/Private contexts follow policy (no customer-specific info leaked)

---

## Out of scope (explicit)
- Building customer-specific incident feeds in Console (per-tenant).
- Publishing detailed infrastructure topology or provider-specific failures.
- Adding new regions to the platform.

---

## Requirements
### Functional requirements
- R1: Each status incident update must select impacted **component(s)** and **region(s)** (cannot post “global API” if the issue is streaming-only in one region).
- R2: Internal signals (error rate, latency percentiles, burn rates) map to components using stable labels.
- R3: Anti-flap / hysteresis rules to avoid rapid toggling during transient spikes.
- R4: Incident tooling drafts updates using templates and incident state, reducing manual writing.
- R5: For Sev0/Sev1, add a lightweight approval option (IC or Support lead) before publishing updates.
- R6: Post-incident summaries can be generated from incident timeline + metrics, then reviewed before publishing.

### Reliability and safety requirements
- S1: Do not over-report impact (avoid “all regions” when only one region is affected).
- S2: Do not under-report impact (avoid “Operational” when a major capability is failing).
- S3: Avoid sensitive details (customer names, tenant IDs, specific capacity constraints, exploit/security specifics).
- S4: Ensure rollback path for taxonomy/mapping changes if they cause incorrect public statuses.

### Copy/tone requirements
- Clear, direct language; avoid speculation.
- Early updates should acknowledge uncertainty.
- Avoid implying SLA credits or contractual remedies.

---

## Success metrics
### Primary
- **TTFU (time-to-first public update):**
  - Target: P50 ≤ 15 min, P90 ≤ 30 min for Sev0/Sev1 incidents where customer impact is confirmed.
- **Status accuracy audit pass rate:**
  - Target: ≥ 95% of audited incidents have correct component(s)/region(s) selected within the first 60 minutes.

### Secondary
- **Support ticket deflection:** decrease in tickets disputing status accuracy (baseline from SUP-28411/28436/28549 cluster).
- **Post-incident summary time-to-publish:**
  - Target: summary published within 5 business days for Sev0/Sev1, within 10 business days for Sev2 (policy finalized in PM-612).
- **Customer sentiment (qualitative):** CS notes from QBRs and procurement/security reviews cite improved transparency.

---

## Rollout plan (phased)
### Phase 0 — Design + governance (Weeks 1–2)
- Finalize component taxonomy + definitions + ownership
- Decide and document source of truth for registry + review process
- Finalize signal standards and anti-flap guidance

Exit criteria:
- Taxonomy doc approved by SRE + Infra + Support/CS + Legal/Security reviewers

### Phase 1 — Implementation (Weeks 3–5)
- Implement component registry + service-to-component mapping + validation/tests
- Add component-tagged metrics and dashboards
- Incident-bot updates: required component/region fields; draft templates; comms lead reminders
- Post-incident summary generator MVP + review workflow

Exit criteria:
- Dogfood in internal incidents with accuracy audits; rollback plan documented

### Phase 2 — Staged rollout (Week 6)
- Internal dogfood → limited public rollout (subset of components/regions) → full rollout
- Comms Lead training session + on-call enablement
- Support macros updated to align with templates

Exit criteria:
- No major accuracy regressions during limited rollout; Support/CS confirms usability

### Phase 3 — Measurement + iteration (Weeks 7–8)
- Weekly accuracy audit job + review meeting
- Tighten mapping rules, templates, and approval flow based on findings

## Risks and mitigations
- Risk: Over-granularity causes confusion or maintenance burden.
  - Mitigation: Start with high-signal splits (Streaming vs Embeddings vs Core API) + top regions; expand only with demonstrated value.
- Risk: Incorrect mapping leads to wrong public status.
  - Mitigation: Schema validation + tests; staged rollout; weekly audits; easy rollback.
- Risk: Increased on-call workload from more components.
  - Mitigation: Incident-bot templates, prefilled fields, dashboards linked from alerts; anti-flap.
- Risk: Sensitive information leaks in post-incident summaries.
  - Mitigation: Strict template guidance; required review for Sev0/Sev1; security/legal sign-off for policy.

---

## Open questions
1) Dedicated/Private public components: do we expose any Dedicated control-plane signals publicly, or keep to generic messaging per PM-612?
2) Latency-only degradations: criteria for “Degraded Performance” vs “Partial Outage” for customer-facing components.
3) Approval workflow: which events require Support lead approval vs IC-only vs no approval.
